President Donald Trump has agreed to grant an immediate visa to the mother of Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old boy originally from Ghana who was shot and killed on his way to school in the Bronx earlier this week, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday.
“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani posted on X. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately.”
The mayor’s office did not immediately specify what kind of visa had been granted when contacted by Gothamist, and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.
Frimpong was shot around 9:30 a.m. on Thursday near Crotona Park in the Bronx, according to police.
Officers who responded found Frimpong with a gunshot to his abdomen and drove him to St. Barnabas Hospital in their patrol car, where he was pronounced dead, police said.
Authorities still have not named or described any suspects, or said what led to the shooting.
Frimpong’s father, Thomas Frimpong, told Gothamist that his son came to the United States to live with him last year.
This story will be updated with more information.

Pre-K busing in downtown Jersey City's hitting a crisis point, parents say
By
Michael Sol Warren
Published Oct 31, 2026 at 12:00 p.m. ET

Michael Sol Warren / Gothamist

Published Oct 31, 2026 at 12:00 p.m. ET
Share

A decadelong economic boom has transformed Jersey City’s Paulus Hook neighborhood into one of the most desirable in the city. But the influx of new families has led to chronic and often chaotic overcrowding at P.S. 16, the elementary school that serves the area.
Toddlers in the school’s Pre-K program have to be bused throughout the city because the building has no room for them. District leaders have said for years that busing pre-K students to other city schools was a temporary solution. But next year, all of the kindergartners at the school — which serves students through the fifth grade — will be bused to other locations as well. The issue has become a constant complaint from frustrated parents speaking at school board and City Council meetings, and it’s become a key issue in Jersey City’s pivotal and crowded school board election.
The school is situated amid brownstones, boutiques and brunch spots, but space is scarce in the area, and any building plan would need to be run by state officials who are grappling with even worse overcrowding in other cities.
That leaves Jersey City leaders weighing options no one likes — including the prospect of shuffling kids around further with redistricting. Jersey City often has worse traffic than Manhattan and local parents say during pickup they often wait in the cold without any sense of when their toddlers will be dropped off.
“ If it was a rainy day, we would be out in the rain. We're out in the sun. We've been out in the snow,” said Renee Perna, who has a pre-K student and a first grader at P.S. 16, also known as the Cornelia F. Bradford School. “ If your 18-month-old had an older sibling getting on the bus, you'd be out here with your infant waiting for the bus.”
For now, parents and officials say, students are left competing for space and attention in classrooms never intended to accommodate so many at once.
“My son is going be in a classroom with something like 35 students next year, and he's been in crowded classes since kindergarten,” said Patrick Carr, the father of a P.S. 16 fifth grader. “He started kindergarten with 30, 31 kids. At this point, kindergartens are upwards of 35 to 40.”
Rapid growth
About 68,000 new housing units have been approved in Jersey City since 2015, then-Mayor Steve Fulop said last year.
Much of that growth has been centered downtown and along the city’s waterfront, the areas served by P.S. 16. Enrollment roughly tripled from 430 students in the 2015-2016 school year, to 1,144 in the 2025-2026 school year.
That’s a drastic change for a school that still operates out of a brick building that opened more than a century ago, when Paulus Hook was far less desirable.
“ It was the poorest section of the city at the time it was built,” Norma Fernandez, the superintendent of Jersey City Public Schools, said.. “It was named after Cornelia Bradford, who was an activist in the community who really fought to educate the children of the lowest working classes.”
Today, Fernandez said, P.S. 16 serves the district's wealthiest and most highly educated families. It’s the only school in the district that doesn’t receive federal assistance funding. And it’s one of the most highly rated, highly sought-after schools in Jersey City.
But just 13 new classrooms have been added to the area, all inside an annex for P.S. 16 that opened in 2021 and was designed to accommodate the school's pre-K students. Fernandez said, by the time it opened, enrollment had grown so much that the space was needed for older grades instead.
The busing dilemma
Parents walk their 3- and 4-year-olds to P.S. 16 every morning to load the kids onto buses that line multiple city blocks, while older students play in the school’s courtyard.
Sometimes cars are parked in bus zones from the night before, so the buses have to double park and disrupt traffic, which is typically at a standstill during rush hour downtown. Parents complain that drivers don’t always respect bus stop signs and crosswalks, even after the city added crossing guards to the area.
Perna describes the scene as “mayhem.” She said the evenings can be worse, because of the uncertainty around when the buses bringing kids back to P.S. 16 will show up.
“ In winter when you've got the snow and the ice, and we're out here waiting, and nobody's updating us,” Perna said.
The Danforth Early Childhood Center in the Greenville neighborhood is the main destination for P.S. 16’s pre-K students. The drive can take 30 minutes or more.
Much of Jersey City's explosive growth has been centered downtown and along the city’s waterfront, the areas served by P.S. 16.
Michael Sol Warren / Gothamist
Fernandez said pre-K students are bused instead of older grades because state regulations on class sizes and facilities mean pre-K takes up more space. And she said the resources inside P.S. 16 are better suited for older kids.
“ P.S. 16 has a beautiful auditorium, has a pool,” Fernandez said. “Those are facilities that are put to better use by the older students.”
Carr said he’s sympathetic to the situation district leaders are facing.
“This is a problem that's created by the city ultimately,” Carr said. “ The city is the entity that is permitting all the construction, and the school district just has to cope.”

The death toll from a deadly e-bike fire continues to rise, police said, after two teenage boys and an adult woman have now died alongside Zion Maine, the boy killed earlier this week in his family’s Bronx apartment.
Fire officials said the battery on an e-bike ignited just before 1 a.m. Wednesday in the kitchen of the family’s 11th-floor apartment. The bike was stored near the front door and blocked the family’s exit.
Maine died at a nearby hospital, city officials said. His father, Courtney Maine, 37, was in stable condition Saturday. The three others hospitalized were Maine’s two sons and his partner Syida Adams, but police did not confirm their identities Saturday.
Tayesha Aiken, 41, has lived in the Patterson Houses, a public housing complex in Mott Haven, for a decade. She said Zion was “loved in the community.”
“Praying and crying is all I’ve been doing,:” she said earlier this week. “I think that’s all we really can do at this point is pray.”
Carol Chen contributed reporting.

Few people have gotten under President Donald Trump’s skin quite the way New York Attorney General Letitia James has.
The Democratic attorney general has long been one of the president’s chief antagonists, suing the Republican’s administration more than 80 times since she took office in 2018 while becoming a frequent target of his ire on social media and at rallies.
Now, James has made her battles with Trump a central part of her campaign to win another four years in office.
“As  I travel all throughout the state of New York and even the country, individuals thank me for standing up and protecting the interest of New Yorkers,” James said in an interview with Gothamist. “They thank me for recognizing that no one is above the law and that we do not bow to kings.”
But if she’s to win on Tuesday, she’ll have to overcome a challenge from Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor who has accused James of being “obsessed with national politics” and politicizing an office that should remain apolitical.
James, the former New York City public advocate who previously served as a city councilmember from Brooklyn, first rose to the attorney general’s office in the middle of Trump’s first term in 2018.
Since then, she has become a legal thorn in the president’s side.
Her lawsuits against the Trump administration — often leading a coalition of Democratic attorneys general from other states — have targeted the president’s actions on everything from immigration enforcement to Medicaid funding to housing grants.
She’s also targeted the president’s business, winning a civil fraud judgement against the Trump administration in 2023 that found it engaged in a scheme to inflate the value of its real-estate holdings to obtain better rates on loans.
But the fraud judgement ultimately became a mixed bag for James. It initially came with a $500 million disgorgement penalty, which a mid-level appeals court later threw out in its entirety. The case remains tied up in the Court of Appeals, the state’s highest court.
Trump’s Department of Justice, meanwhile, tried to prosecute James for alleged mortgage fraud on a home occupied by a family member in Virginia. A court threw out the indictment.
James said her legal clashes with Trump are a sign that she’s willing to take on powerful people when their interests clash with those of New Yorkers. She said voters have responded warmly to her legal battles with Trump.
Republican attorney general candidate Saritha Komatireddy appears at an event with Bruce Blakeman, the Republican candidate for New York governor, where they criticized the state's sanctuary policies.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
Komatireddy, meanwhile, has tried to keep the focus of her campaign on James, not the president.
The Republican has said she voted for Trump but has emphasized that she worked in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for New York’s Eastern District under three presidents — Trump, Barack Obama and Joe Biden. She also served as chief of staff to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration under Biden.
“I've always protected New York and protected Americans by working with Democrats and Republicans and for Democrats and Republicans,” Komatireddy said in an interview with Gothamist. “I have no problem doing that. Not everything has to be partisan.”
Komatiredddy said she would reorganize the attorney general’s office to have more of a focus on crime and fraud — two areas where she says James has been lacking.
“ This is just about having competent government,” she said. “People are tired of elected officials using the office for their own personal benefit instead of the benefit of New Yorkers, and I'm actually here to make New Yorkers' lives better for all of us.”
Komatireddy has experienced a fundraising bump following her lone debate with James earlier this month, when the Republican’s aggressive, direct critiques of James landed several clips that bounced around certain corners of the internet. Those clips were further boosted by Trump, who praised Komatireddy’s performance on his Truth Social platform without mentioning her by name.
In the 11 days following the debate, Komitareddy raised about $500,000, not counting public matching funds. In the three months prior to that, she raised about $700,000, according to state disclosure records.
“I'm walking down the road in [the New York City Columbus Day] parade and people are reaching out to shake my hand, shouting out saying, ‘You did a great job. I'm voting for you,'” Komatireddy said. “Someone came up to me and said, ‘Can I donate to your campaign?’”
James, meanwhile, says Komatireddy’s focus on street crime shows a fundamental misunderstanding of the job.
The attorney general’s office has traditionally focused on civil issues, not local crimes. Under James, that has included work obtaining financial settlements from opioid manufacturers and distributors for their role in the opioid crisis, as well as from Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta to settle claims that they intentionally got kids hooked on the social-media platforms.
Local district attorneys, on the other hand, are generally charged with prosecuting crimes like assault, theft and drug trafficking.

Outreach worker Felipe Ramos said one of the hardest parts of his job is seeing himself in those he helps: the people sleeping on New York City's streets.
Ramos has also cycled through homelessness, incarceration and a history of mental illness. But he said his past is now his superpower as he crisscrosses Manhattan every day, trying to get New Yorkers to come inside.
“We can say to our clients, ‘Hey, I know exactly what you're feeling. … I'm actually going to feel it with you in this moment, and then when you're ready, we're going to come up with a detailed plan to get you out of this feeling,’” he said.
“It's probably the most genuine form of connection that we can build.”
Ramos is part of the Neighborhood Navigators program, started by the Manhattan district attorney’s office to bring street homeless New Yorkers inside and prevent them from entering the criminal justice system. The Mamdani administration this year awarded the program $1.25 million in funding as it develops a citywide plan to combat homelessness.
It’s part of a growing citywide effort to interrupt the cycle of New Yorkers moving between the street, the hospital and the shelter system. Nearly 5,000 people slept in parks, subway stations or the street this year — the highest number recorded in more than a decade.
“It’s far more powerful to get people who have walked in these shoes,” Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg told Gothamist. “And recognize the significance of what that individual engagement means to them because they know what it meant to them.”
The city’s street outreach system can be uncoordinated, leaving groups working in silos or overwhelming the very people they’re trying to help, advocates said. It’s why elected leaders and other stakeholders are calling on the city to streamline its approach and double down on programs that show results.
Bragg said the Neighborhood Navigators approach is different because it hires workers with similar experiences to form closer relationships with chronically homeless people and because of the amount of time workers spend with those they help, including accompanying them to appointments or doctor’s offices.
“Instead of, ‘What's wrong with you?’ We ask, ‘What happened to you?’” said Rocio Santos, program director of the Neighborhood Navigators.
“Looking them in their face, taking the time to [say], ‘Hey, how are you? We noticed you don't have shoes. Is there anything that we can support you with?’”
Bragg said his office decided to start its own street outreach program after realizing people were falling through the cracks between various providers and city agencies. He said he ultimately wants to prevent people from ever landing in court.
The DA’s office hired nonprofit The Bridge to implement the program in certain neighborhoods in 2024, using forfeiture funds. More than 175 people have been placed in housing since.
“Sometimes the navigators will be with someone for an entire day, just making sure that they get into their housing placement or to an inpatient substance use treatment program,” said Lauren Curatolo, a deputy division chief at the Manhattan DA's office.
The program works in certain areas of the city including Central and East Harlem; Chinatown and the Lower East Side; Washington Heights and Inwood; and Midtown West, Hell's Kitchen and Chelsea.
Barbara Blair, president of the Garment District Alliance, said the Neighborhood Navigators “do a good job of following people” from point A to point B. She said the business improvement district also hired the navigators to perform outreach in the area.
“I don't want you dumping someone off at the hospital and then you don't hear from them again, you don't see them again until they're back on the street,” Blair said.
In one case, the Neighborhood Navigators helped a 58-year-old Harlem man get his public benefits reinstated, staying with him at the city’s benefits office all day. In another case, they were able to connect a 67-year-old living in Lower Manhattan to a supportive housing unit in less than three weeks. The man also received a psychiatric evaluation and medication to remain stable.
Ramos said the Neighborhood Navigators have a good reputation among people living on the street and that helps them make inroads. So if they say they’ll pick someone up from the hospital at 6 a.m., they’ll be there at 6 a.m.
“Recovery isn't comfortable, but it's attainable. So being willing to listen to them and being able to hold their hand through the hard parts is what'll continue to make things systematically better,” he said.
The group does not have access to the city’s database of engagements between outreach workers and homeless people. Only providers contracted by the Department of Homeless Services do, and that can make collaboration with other groups difficult.
But the Navigators said they create networks in each neighborhood. They know whom they can lean on for substance abuse programs, shelter, medical care or mental health.
“ We brought the personal back into this type of work,” said Santos. “We're able to pick up the phone at any given point and reach those individuals that could support and help our clients.”

A woman who went out for a jog Friday evening is in critical condition, police said, after being stabbed in the neck and left on a waterfront trail in Brooklyn's Bath Beach neighborhood.
Just after 8 p.m. officials said they received a call regarding a person stabbed on a bike path near Bay Parkway and Cropsey Avenue in Bath Beach.
Police found the 28-year-old woman with a stab wound to the neck and transported her to NYU Langone where she was listed in critical condition as of 9:30 Saturday morning.
No arrests have been made and authorities were not able to give a description of a suspect.

When Daniel Cho crosses the finish line of this year’s New York City Marathon, he’ll join more than 18,000 first-time runners to do so.
But this time last year, he was part of a very different statistic.
Cho was standing on the platform of the Bowery J/Z train station at around 4 p.m. on Oct. 29, 2025. He was on his way to collect a racing t-shirt for his first-ever marathon from a non-profit group he was helping to raise money for low-income Asian youths.
A stranger approached him on the platform and punched him in the face, shouting a racist slur. Cho ended up on the train tracks.
“I turned around to look if there was a train coming. [The tunnel] was pitch black, and so I said, ‘OK, get it together, and you're gonna be able to figure it out,’” Cho said.
He climbed back onto the platform, called 911, and gave the police a detailed description that helped them quickly catch his assailant. But in an instant, Cho, 46, became one of more than 29,800 people who would experience a serious physical assault somewhere in the city in 2025.
The arrest of his perpetrator was only the beginning of Cho’s mental and physical journey toward recovery. With multiple fractures to his right cheekbone, nerve damage along his eye socket and only four days to go before the race, doctors told him to cancel his marathon bid.
In the months that followed, he’d endure surgery to install a titanium plate in his face, log hours of work with a therapist to overcome lingering post-traumatic stress disorder, and shuttle to acupuncture treatments to tackle persistent numbness.
Daniel Cho shortly after he was punched and thrown onto subway tracks.
Courtesy of Daniel Cho
In early spring, Cho decided he was ready to run again — and hoped to take another shot at New York City’s iconic race.
“ Both marathon training and recovery from violence, or just a crime, ask for the same things: resilience, motivation, mental fortitude,” he said. “So I've been able to redefine that strength.”
While many of the city’s major violent crimes have declined significantly this year, felony assaults — the kind of attacks that leave people with serious injuries — have remained confoundingly high. According to the most recent NYPD data, there have been 165 more felony assaults reported citywide this year than the same time period last year, bucking the decreases in other kinds of offenses.
The same man who punched Cho was allegedly involved in four other anti-Asian attacks that same day, according to Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. So far this year there have been 548 felony assaults in transit, up from 490 at this time last year; an 11% increase.
The MTA declined to comment on Cho’s attack or on the spike in assaults on its system.
Cho, who works for the New York City Campaign Finance Board, was originally running the marathon to raise money for Apex for Youth: a nonprofit headquartered in Manhattan’s Chinatown that provides resources and mentorship to young Asian Americans from low-income backgrounds. Now, he said, he is also running to raise awareness about the prevalence of similar attacks, to spread hope to other survivors, and to reclaim his sense of safety and community in the city he loves.
Daniel Cho is back.
Brittany Kriegstein/Gothamist
“I was running for kids who are learning to trust this city to nurture and protect their futures. And then I had to learn to trust the city again myself with every commute, with every subway ride,” he said.
Cho’s message to other survivors is to treat recovery like marathon training: a long process with ups and downs, twists and turns, progress and setbacks.
“Find your own healing journey,” he said. “Don’t be afraid to tell your story…and my last thing is, create space for that intentional rest.”
On marathon day, Cho said he is most looking forward to “taking it all in,” “finding joy in the struggle,” and  seeing his wife and two kids at mile 14. He said the race provides a unique opportunity for people from all walks of life to find common ground with strangers.
“ New York is a place for everyone, like nowhere else in the world, and the city belongs to all of us,” he said. “Hopefully we can lift each other up.”
This story has been updated to clarify the item Cho was collecting and the nature of his attack.

The city says that there are no more traces of asbestos at Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses.
A steam leak left asbestos-laden residue on some of the exterior walls at 502 and 504 Marcy Ave., part of the New York City Housing Authority complex in Bedford-Stuyvesant.
NYCHA and the city Department of Environmental Protection visited the site on Thursday after some residents said they had been complaining for weeks.
Some buildings also lost heat and hot water because of the issue.
The city said it has relocated four of the 23 households residing near the asbestos-laden walls until Oct. 31, while another household opted to stay with family.
The city also confirmed that all 24 air monitors installed in the apartments along the affected wall tested negative for asbestos on Friday.
Similar tests at the daycare, management office and exterior of Buildings 4 and 17 also tested negative.
The city also restored heat and hot water at four of the affected buildings on Thursday around 11:30 p.m., followed by the remaining five buildings just after midnight.
While residents have already received notices about the negative test results, the city said it will continue to test all exterior areas in the complex for asbestos.
"To date, all air monitoring test results have been negative for asbestos, including exterior and interior apartment testing, and air monitoring of exterior areas will continue until remediation is complete,” NYCHA spokesperson Andrew Sklar said.
The city’s environmental protection department has already cleaned up the sidewalk, cars and building facade at Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses, but has yet to finish the courtyard.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the matter.
